track.name: product
track.label: Product & Strategy
track.summary: Learn how product managers uncover real customer problems, prioritize and roadmap ruthlessly, set product strategy, and partner with engineering and design to ship outcomes that move the metrics that matter.

phases.title: What Product Managers Actually Do
phases.description: What the PM role actually covers day to day, and how it differs from product owner and project manager roles.

phases.title: Product Discovery
phases.description: Talk to real customers, validate problems before solutions, and build the habit of continuous discovery.

phases.title: Prioritization & Roadmapping
phases.description: Turn a long list of ideas into a defensible priority order and a roadmap stakeholders can trust.

phases.title: Product Strategy
phases.description: Set a product vision, position against competitors, and connect day-to-day work to a coherent strategy.

phases.title: Working with Engineering & Design
phases.description: Write specs engineers can build from, speak the language of agile delivery, and collaborate as a true product trio.

phases.title: Product Metrics & Experimentation
phases.description: Pick metrics that actually reflect customer value, and use experiments instead of opinions to settle debates.

topics.title: What Product Managers Actually Do
topics.description: What the product manager role covers, and why it's centered on solving customer problems rather than managing a backlog.

steps.t: List the actual problems PMs solve
steps.d: Write down three specific customer problems a PM on your team discovered this month, not feature requests or technical tasks.
Compare a PM who spent the week on customer interviews against one who organized sprint stories, and name the difference in what each one accomplished.
Plan a week's schedule for a PM at your company or a company you know well, filling it with the activities that actually surface customer problems.

steps.t: Audit a PRD for problem focus
steps.d: Open a real product requirements document from your company and underline every sentence that references a customer problem versus every sentence that describes features.
Review your team's last month of work and identify at least one piece of work that doesn't clearly connect to solving a customer problem.

topics.title: PM vs. Product Owner vs. Project Manager
topics.description: How these three commonly-confused titles differ in scope, focus, and day-to-day responsibilities.

steps.d: Write a one-sentence definition of what a Product Manager, a Product Owner, and a Project Manager each own in your organization or one you know.
Describe what a PM, PO, and PM each actually spend their time on in a typical week, with at least one concrete example per role.
Draw a table showing who decides on roadmap priorities, who decides on implementation approach, and who tracks delivery status in your org.

steps.t: Identify role overlap in your org
steps.d: Name one decision at your company that the PM and PO both influence, and describe why the overlap exists.
Have a conversation with your engineering and design leads where you confirm how your company actually uses the titles PM, PO, and PM in practice.

topics.title: Empowered Product Teams vs. Feature Teams
topics.description: The difference between teams handed a list of features to build and teams handed problems to solve.

steps.d: Explain what happens when a team is handed a list of features to build instead of problems to solve, with a real example from your industry.
Diagram how a team that owns a customer problem (not a feature list) actually goes from problem to solution, including discovery and iteration.
Describe a product or team you know that operates as feature-focused, and contrast it with one that's problem-focused — what ships differently.
Name the three main responsibilities a PM has when leading an empowered team versus leading a feature-delivery team.
Determine whether your team is feature-focused or problem-focused by looking at a recent release and asking what decided what shipped.

topics.title: Finding People to Interview
topics.description: The step before discovery: who to talk to, how to reach them, and how to screen out the wrong ones.

steps.d: Three or four questions that separate someone who has the problem from someone who merely finds it interesting.

steps.t: List five places those people already are
steps.d: A subreddit, a WhatsApp group, a trade body, your own support inbox, a conference attendee list. Name actual ones.

steps.t: Write the ask in three sentences
steps.d: Who you are, what you want to learn, how long it takes. No pitch — a pitch gets you a polite yes and a useless interview.
Assume one no-show. Send a calendar invite rather than agreeing a time in a thread.

steps.t: Check who you did not reach
steps.d: After five interviews, write down which kind of user never replied. That absence will bias everything you conclude.

topics.title: Customer Interviews & Problem Discovery
topics.description: How to talk to customers in a way that surfaces real problems instead of confirming what you already believed.

steps.d: Write out how you'd recruit and schedule three customers to talk about a specific problem your product aims to solve.
Write five questions you'd ask in a customer interview that can't be answered yes-or-no and that let them talk about their actual workflow.
Run an interview with a customer (or someone in your target user role) and document what surprised you about their process that contradicted your assumptions.
Review your interview notes and highlight every moment you heard something that contradicted what you believed going in.
Write two lists from your interview — one of customer problems they mentioned, one of solutions they suggested — and notice which ones are actually the same problem reframed.

topics.title: Continuous Discovery Habits
topics.description: Building a weekly cadence of small customer touchpoints instead of one big research phase before launch.

steps.t: Commit to a weekly touchpoint schedule
steps.d: Block 90 minutes every week for customer conversations and write down how many prospects or customers you'll reach each month.
Pick a lightweight format (Slack interview, 15-minute call, or customer feedback form) and commit to running it every single week for two months.
After five customer conversations, write down the three most common problems you've heard and count how many customers mentioned each one.
Find a feature your team launched in the last year and ask customers (in discovery) whether they'd seen the problem that feature solves, and how many said yes.
After eight weeks, count the number of customer conversations you actually had and identify which ones changed what you were planning to build.

topics.title: Validating Problems Before Solutions
topics.description: Using lightweight opportunity assessments to decide whether a problem is worth solving before committing engineering time.

steps.d: Take one problem you've heard from customers and score it on reach (how many have it), impact (how much it affects them), and confidence (how sure you are).
Sketch three different solutions to that problem and estimate the effort required to build each one, then calculate impact-per-effort ratio.
Document your judgment on the problem in a one-page assessment that includes the problem, how many customers have it, and why it's worth solving right now.
Show your assessment to an engineer or leader who doesn't think this problem matters and try to change their mind using only the evidence you've collected.
Using your assessment, decide whether your team will actually work on this problem, and write down what evidence would have changed your decision.

topics.title: RICE & Prioritization Frameworks
topics.description: Scoring competing ideas on reach, impact, confidence, and effort instead of prioritizing by opinion or seniority.

steps.d: Calculate a RICE score for three competing ideas: reach (number of users impacted), impact (how much each user benefits), confidence (your certainty), effort (engineer-weeks required).
Gather your product and engineering leads, score three competing ideas as a group using RICE, and note where your estimates diverged.
Rank those same three ideas the way your team used to (by opinion, executive vote, or squeaky-wheel), then compare to RICE — what changed position.
Look at your three RICE scores and for each, write down the assumption you're least confident about (like actual reach or actual effort).
Use RICE to rank your top ten competing ideas, and present the ranking to your team with one sentence explaining why the top item won.

topics.title: Opportunity Solution Trees
topics.description: Mapping opportunities and solutions visually so a team can see and debate its options instead of jumping to one idea.

steps.d: List five customer problems your team has identified (from discovery work), then identify three to five solutions for each problem.
Draw an opportunity-solution tree on a whiteboard or in Figma with your opportunities at the top, solutions in the middle, and initiatives at the bottom.
Look at your tree and notice whether you have multiple solutions per opportunity, whether some opportunities have no solutions yet, and whether some solutions solve multiple problems.
Explain your tree to an engineer or executive who hasn't seen it and ask them to point out the first opportunity they'd attack.
Use your opportunity-solution tree to rank your initiatives for the next quarter and show how each initiative addresses one of your top opportunities.

topics.title: Outcome-Based Roadmapping
topics.description: Building roadmaps around outcomes and time horizons instead of a fixed list of features and dates.

steps.d: Write your team's last three shipped features as outputs, then rewrite each as an outcome (what changed for customers, not what shipped).
Define what 'now' (next 6 weeks), 'next' (6-12 weeks), and 'later' (12+ months) mean in terms of your product roadmap and company strategy.
Write a one-page roadmap with three to four outcomes per time horizon (now, next, later) instead of listing specific features.
Show your outcome-based roadmap to your CFO, CEO, or board and ask them what outcomes they'd prioritize differently.
Take your 'now' outcomes and write a list of the actual features or work that would prove each outcome landed.

topics.title: Product Vision & Strategy Fundamentals
topics.description: The difference between a multi-year vision, a strategy, and the tactics that execute it.

steps.d: Write a three-to-five-year vision statement for your product that describes the change in the world when your product succeeds.
Take your vision, identify three strategic choices (like market segment or pricing model) that would get you there, then list the tactics (features or initiatives) that execute each.
Review your vision to a team member who doesn't work on this product and ask them to summarize it back to you — do they get it right.
Take three items on your engineering roadmap and trace each one upward to the strategy and then to the vision — can you draw a clear line.
Compare your written vision and strategy against the actual work your team is doing — identify at least one piece of work that doesn't clearly connect to the vision.

topics.title: Competitive Positioning & Market Analysis
topics.description: Framing a product against competitive alternatives so the right customers immediately understand its value.

steps.d: List every company or product that a customer might choose instead of yours, including not direct competitors but adjacent solutions.
For each competitor, write one sentence describing why customers would pick your product instead — focus on what you're better at or different about.
Compose a single paragraph saying who your product is for, what problem it solves better than alternatives, and why customers should believe that.
Review your website, your app's first-time-user experience, and your pitch deck — compare to your positioning statement and identify what's not aligned.
Show your positioning statement and one competitor's positioning to three prospects in your target market and ask which they find more compelling and why.

topics.title: Strategy Frameworks in Practice
topics.description: Applying a diagnosis-guiding policy-actions structure to tell a good strategy from a list of goals dressed up as one.

steps.d: Write a clear, one-sentence diagnosis of the customer problem your strategy aims to solve (e.g., 'remote teams spend 30% of meetings waiting for people to find the right document').
Write one sentence explaining the strategic principle that guides decisions (e.g., 'we make it so obvious what to search for that finding never takes more than 10 seconds').
Write four to six specific initiatives that all flow from your diagnosis and policy — show how each one reinforces the others.
Compare your diagnosis-policy-actions structure against your actual roadmap and identify at least one initiative that doesn't clearly support your policy.
Explain your strategy to someone skeptical and show how all three parts (diagnosis, policy, actions) work together to address the customer problem.

topics.title: Writing PRDs & Specs
topics.description: Writing a requirements document that aligns a team around the problem and success criteria, not just a feature list.

steps.d: Before describing how to build a feature, write down exactly how you'd know the feature succeeded (measurable outcome, not 'users like it').
Compose a one-paragraph description of the customer problem you're solving, why it matters, and who has it — the 'why' before the 'what'.
Describe the most important user workflow step-by-step (at least five steps) — what does the user do first, what happens next, what decides when they're done.
Write the workflow for when everything works normally, then write three scenarios where something goes wrong or unusual and how your spec handles each.
Give your PRD to an engineer and ask them to summarize the problem, the success criteria, and what they'd build first — check if they got it right.

topics.title: Agile & Scrum Basics for PMs
topics.description: The ceremonies, roles, and vocabulary of Scrum a PM needs to work effectively with an agile engineering team.

topics.title: Cross-Functional Collaboration
topics.description: Working as a true trio with design and engineering so decisions get made together, not handed off in sequence.

steps.d: Schedule a weekly 30-minute meeting with your design and engineering leads and attend it for the next eight weeks without skipping.
Take the next feature you're about to build and instead of handing design a finished spec, spend two sessions exploring the problem together before sketching solutions.
Attend your team's design critique, and for at least two critiques, come prepared with feedback focused on the problem the design solves, not aesthetics.
Take one architectural or interaction choice that's ambiguous (where two reasonable solutions both work) and make the call together as a trio, documenting why.
After four weeks of trio work, ask both your design and engineering leads whether decisions feel more aligned than they did before.

topics.title: North Star Metrics & Product Metrics
topics.description: Choosing a single metric that captures customer value, and the input metrics that actually move it.

steps.d: Write down the five most important things customers actually do in your product each week (e.g., 'send a message', 'view a list', 'create a document').
For each behavior, write down what you'd measure to know whether customers are getting value (not activity, but value).
Pick one metric, then trace backward and ask 'why do we care if this goes up' at least three times until you reach the actual customer benefit.
Write a single metric that best captures whether your product is delivering value to customers, and describe why you'd use this one over all others.
List your North Star metric, then write four to five input metrics (things you can influence more directly) that you think drive the North Star.

topics.title: A/B Testing Fundamentals for PMs
topics.description: The basics of running a valid experiment so a launch decision rests on evidence instead of the loudest opinion in the room.

steps.d: Write a complete hypothesis: 'If we change X, then Y metric will increase by Z%, because customers will Z'.
For your hypothesis, describe the control group, the treatment group, what version they each see, and how long the test should run to get a reliable answer.
Before running the experiment, write down whether you think your hypothesis is true and exactly how confident you are (as a percentage).
Actually run an A/B test on a feature (even a small internal one) and collect the results for at least 50 people per group.
After the test, compare your prediction to the actual results and write down what surprised you and what that means for the next test.
